query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a low concentration of Sn (e.g., around 3–5 at.%, introduced during melting) to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance by promoting the formation of a continuous, Sn‐enriched protective oxide scale that retards oxygen ingress during high‐temperature exposure, while preserving the alloy’s inherent room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr with a single BCC solid-solution microstructure that exhibits 8–16% tensile ductility at room temperature and yield strengths in the range of 163–530 MPa at elevated temperatures, but suffers from inadequate oxygen resistance (pesting) in air.
generation.intervention: Introduce a low, controlled addition of Sn (approximately 3–5 at.%) during the alloy melting process.
generation.conditions: Exposure to laboratory air at around 800 °C for approximately 5 hours. Mechanical performance evaluations should be conducted at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (up to about 1000 °C) under strain rates on the order of 10^(-4) to 10^(-2) s^(-1).
generation.structural_mediator: The development of a continuous, adherent Sn-enriched oxide scale along the surface (and possibly along grain boundaries) that acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
generation.mechanism: Sn acts as a reactive element that preferentially oxidizes at high temperature, forming a protective layer that limits the ingress of oxygen. This reactive element effect suppresses pest oxidation without altering the beneficial single-phase BCC microstructure responsible for the alloy’s balanced mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped alloy, the Sn-doped equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr is expected to exhibit a significantly reduced rate of pest oxidation under a 5-hour air exposure at 800 °C, while retaining similar room-temperature ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa).
generation.baseline: The untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy, although possessing useful mechanical properties, shows rapid pest oxidation under similar high-temperature air exposures.
generation.boundary: This performance improvement is anticipated only if the Sn addition is maintained at low levels (around 3–5 at.%) to avoid forming secondary phases that could detrimentally affect the alloy properties. The hypothesis applies to as-cast samples exposed to air in the 800–1000 °C range for durations up to about 5 hours.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies in related Nb-silicide-based systems support the beneficial role of low Sn additions in improving oxidation resistance, direct evidence for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr is limited, warranting experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy samples by vacuum arc melting: one group modified with ~3–5 at.% Sn and a control group without Sn. Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours under identical conditions. After exposure, conduct microstructural analysis (using SEM coupled with EDS) to evaluate the formation and integrity of the oxide scale and assess signs of pest oxidation. In parallel, perform tensile tests at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (up to 1000 °C) using similar strain rates to compare mechanical performance.
measurements: Continuity and composition of the oxide scale
Degree of pest oxidation (e.g., presence of microcracks, scale spallation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sn-doped alloy fails to form a continuous, protective Sn-enriched oxide scale or if it does not exhibit a significant reduction in pest oxidation compared to the undoped alloy, or if its mechanical properties (ductility or yield strength) are markedly degraded, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Structural metallic materials for applications at high temperatures must have a balance of mechanical properties and oxidation resistance. Coated and internally cooled Ni-based superalloys are used in gas turbine engines close to their high temperature limit, which is imposed by the melting temperature of Ni. The search for new alloys with similar or better capabilities at higher temperatures has concentrated on Nb-silicide based alloys that have lower densities, significantly higher solidus temperatures in excess of 1900 °C and can offer notable mechanical properties []. For example, some of these alloys can have compressive yield strength of about 1800 MPa at room temperature, 1200 MPa at 1000 °C and 500 MPa at 1200 °C []. The oxidation resistance of Nb-silicide based alloys was improved dramatically when the key alloying elements Al, Cr, Si, and Ti were in synergy with other transition and refractory metals, for example Hf, Mo, and simple metal and metalloid elements, e.g., Sn [,,,,]. In the case of Sn, the early research [,] concentrated on alloys where its concentration was low to avoid the formation of the A15-Nb3Sn compound. In 2007, Geng et al [] reported that the addition

The research on the oxidation of Nb-silicide-based alloys would suggest (a) that Ge and/or Sn are needed to suppress pest oxidation, and (b) that, when these alloying additions were present individually or simultaneously in the alloys, the spallation of their scales at high temperatures was not suppressed. It is now well established that Ge or Sn has an effect on macrosegregation and can also reduce the liquidus temperature of the alloy. Alloying with Sn can affect the stability of the Nbss but not the alloying with Ge, which can, however, significantly reduce the cracking of the substrate below the scale/substrate interface []. Unfortunately, from the oxidation research on multicomponent Nb-silicide-based alloys, it is not clear whether it was the synergy of Sn or Ge individually or simultaneously with Al, Cr, Si, and Ti that improved oxidation resistance, or whether the presence of oxygen scavenging Hf with/without transition and refractory metals and with some or all of the aforementioned elements was essential for increasing the oxidation resistance.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of aluminum to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance by promoting the in situ formation of a protective alumina scale during high-temperature exposure.
drafts.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy with demonstrated good room- and high-temperature mechanical performance but poor oxygen resistance.
drafts.intervention: Introduce a small aluminum doping (on the order of a few atomic percent, e.g., 3–5 at%) into the alloy composition.
drafts.conditions: Exposure in air at approximately 800 °C for a duration of about 5 hours, under mechanical conditions that preserve both room-temperature ductility and high-temperature strength.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense, adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale on the alloy surface that retards oxygen penetration.
drafts.mechanism: At high temperature, aluminum segregates at the surface and oxidizes preferentially to form a slow-growing, protective alumina scale. This scale minimizes further oxygen ingress (thus reducing pesting) while leaving the alloy's bulk microstructure and mechanical properties largely intact.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The aluminum-doped equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will exhibit markedly improved oxidation resistance (i.e., delayed onset of extensive oxidation/pesting) relative to the untreated alloy, while maintaining its useful mechanical performance across the temperature range.
drafts.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr shows inadequate oxygen resistance in air at 800 °C during 5-hour exposures despite having good tensile ductility at room temperature and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies to cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloys subjected to high-temperature oxidation in air (around 800 °C to 1000 °C) for durations on the order of 5 hours, with aluminum additions kept low enough (∼3–5 at%) to avoid altering the beneficial mechanical properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Manufacture two sets of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy samples, one set with 3–5 at% aluminum doping and one untreated control. Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours under identical mechanical loading conditions. After exposure, conduct surface characterization (using SEM, EDS, and XRD) to confirm the formation and integrity of the alumina scale, and perform mechanical tests (e.g., room-temperature tensile tests and high-temperature yield strength measurements) to compare performance.
measurements: Surface oxide layer thickness and composition
Integrity and adherence of the oxide scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the aluminum-doped samples do not show a significant improvement in oxidation resistance (i.e., no formation of a protective alumina scale or no reduction in oxidation-induced degradation) compared to the untreated control, or if the aluminum addition adversely affects the mechanical performance beyond acceptable limits.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a small aluminum addition into the equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy will form a protective alumina (Al2O3) scale at high temperatures that improves oxygen resistance while preserving the alloy’s useful mechanical properties.
drafts.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibiting 8–16% RT tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength but inadequate oxygen resistance.
drafts.intervention: Microalloying the alloy with a low concentration (e.g., ~2 atomic percent) of aluminum, with the composition adjusted accordingly.
drafts.conditions: Exposure in air at 800 °C for 5 hours, with mechanical property assessments conducted at room temperature and up to 1000 °C under strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of a thin, continuous, adherent protective alumina (Al2O3) scale on the alloy surface.
drafts.mechanism: The aluminum addition is expected to preferentially oxidize at elevated temperatures, producing an alumina layer that retards further oxygen ingress and suppresses rapid oxidation (pesting) without significantly degrading the underlying mechanical integrity.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Improved oxygen resistance manifested as reduced oxidation rates and elimination of pesting during prolonged high-temperature air exposure, while retaining the alloy’s original room- and high-temperature mechanical performance.
drafts.baseline: Untreated equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy, which suffers from rapid oxidation and pesting under similar conditions.
drafts.boundary: Effectiveness is predicted for continuous air exposures at temperatures from 800 °C up to 1000 °C over durations similar to 5 hours; mechanical performance should remain within the performance window of the untreated alloy.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one group of the untreated equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy and a second group with ~2 atomic percent aluminum added (with the balance adjusted to maintain near-equiatomic ratios). Subject both groups to oxidation tests by exposing them in laboratory air at 800 °C for 5 hours. Parallel mechanical tests should be performed at room temperature and at 1000 °C (under strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1) to assess tensile ductility and yield strength.
measurements: Mass gain due to oxidation (thermogravimetric analysis)
Surface and cross-sectional microstructural evaluation (scanning electron microscopy with EDS) to verify the presence and integrity of the alumina scale
Quantitative assessment of pesting or surface degradation
Tensile ductility and yield strength measurements at the specified temperatures and strain rates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-containing alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (e.g., similar or greater mass gain and evidence of pesting) compared to the untreated alloy, or if its mechanical properties fall outside the performance range of the untreated alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of Sn as a trace alloying element to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance at high temperatures without deteriorating its favorable mechanical properties.
drafts.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr with a single BCC solid-solution structure exhibiting 8–16% room‐temperature tensile ductility and sufficient high‐temperature yield strength.
drafts.intervention: Introduce a low (e.g., 2–5 atomic %) Sn addition during alloy melting to form a Sn-doped variant.
drafts.conditions: Exposure in air at temperatures between 800 °C and 1000 °C for at least 5 hours under conditions representative of high-temperature mechanical testing (strain rates of 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(−1)), while retaining the as-cast microstructure.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, adherent Sn-enriched oxide scale at the surface and along grain boundaries that retards oxygen ingress and suppresses pest oxidation.
drafts.mechanism: The Sn addition acts as a reactive element that preferentially oxidizes to form a protective oxide (or modifies the oxide‐scale adhesion) that seals the surface and grain boundaries. This limits oxygen diffusion into the bulk, thereby suppressing the pesting phenomenon while leaving the primary BCC phase and mechanical characteristics largely intact.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped alloy, the Sn-doped equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will show significantly reduced pest oxidation (fewer microcracks and less degradation after 5 h air exposure at 800 °C to 1000 °C) while maintaining similar room-temperature ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa).
drafts.baseline: The untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibits inadequate oxygen resistance (pesting) under high-temperature air exposures despite its useful mechanical performance.
drafts.boundary: This effect is expected provided that the Sn addition remains low enough to avoid significant phase changes or precipitation that would otherwise alter the alloy's intrinsic strength and ductility; tests should be limited to as-cast conditions and air exposures at 800–1000 °C for up to 5 hours.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloys by vacuum arc melting: one set with a trace addition of 2–5 at.% Sn and a control set without Sn. Subject both sets to air exposure at 800 °C (and separately at 1000 °C) for 5 hours under identical conditions. After exposure, assess the surface and cross-sectional microstructures via SEM/EDS to evaluate oxide scale continuity and evidence of pesting, and conduct tensile tests at room temperature and high temperatures (using similar strain rates) to compare mechanical properties.
measurements: Extent and morphology of oxide scale and pest oxidation (via microscopy and compositional analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sn-doped alloy exhibits oxide scale integrity and a significant reduction in pest oxidation relative to the undoped alloy while showing comparable mechanical properties, the hypothesis is supported. However, if the Sn-doped alloy shows no improvement in oxidation resistance or if its mechanical properties (ductility/strength) are substantially degraded compared to the undoped alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of tin (Sn) to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance at high temperatures by promoting the formation of a continuous, adherent Sn-enriched surface scale that retards oxygen ingress without compromising its room‐temperature ductility or high‐temperature strength.
drafts.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
drafts.intervention: Introduce a small, controlled addition of Sn (e.g., on the order of 3–5 atomic percent) into the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy during melting.
drafts.conditions: The modified alloy is exposed to air at 800 °C for a duration of 5 hours. Mechanical tests should be carried out both at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (around 800–1000 °C) to verify performance.
drafts.structural_mediator: A finely dispersed, Sn-enriched surface scale or interfacial layer that forms during high-temperature oxidation and acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
drafts.mechanism: Sn, acting as a reactive element, segregates to the surface during oxidation and improves scale adhesion. The protective scale limits oxygen penetration (especially along grain boundaries), thereby preventing pest oxidation while preserving the inherent solid-solution microstructure responsible for the alloy’s good mechanical properties.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated HfNbTaTiZr alloy, the Sn-modified alloy will show significantly reduced oxidation (i.e., suppression of pest oxidation) during a 5-hour exposure at 800 °C, while retaining its useful room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
drafts.baseline: The equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy in the as-cast state, which exhibits inadequate oxygen resistance (with evidence of pest oxidation at 800 °C), despite possessing good mechanical properties.
drafts.boundary: This intervention is applicable to as-cast, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr alloys exposed to atmospheric air at temperatures around 800 °C for durations up to several hours; results may differ if used in coated or heavily processed alloys, or under significantly different atmospheric or thermal conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) the baseline equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr and (2) an Sn-modified variant with 3–5 at.% Sn. Subject both sets to a 5-hour air exposure at 800 °C. Following oxidation, assess the surface oxide scale (thickness, continuity, and adhesion) via microscopy and spectroscopy, and measure mechanical properties (room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength).
measurements: Surface oxide scale characterization (SEM, EDS, XRD) to determine scale morphology and composition.
Weight gain measurements to quantify oxidation rate.
Room-temperature tensile tests to measure ductility.
High-temperature tensile or creep tests to assess yield strength at 800–1000 °C.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sn-modified alloy does not show a significant improvement in oxidation resistance (e.g., no reduction in pest oxidation signs, similar or increased oxidation rate, or compromised mechanical properties compared to the baseline), then the hypothesis is falsified.
